slides.title: ENGINEERING PRINCIPLES
slides.sectionSubtitle: How Kepler worked as one precision instrument.
slides.slideTitle: Capturing Starlight and Measuring Its Secrets
slides.text: Parallel rays of starlight enter the telescope, strike its 1.4-meter concave primary mirror, and reflect toward the prime focus. There, the beam converges onto a curved focal-plane mosaic of 42 charge-coupled device detectors. Photons striking the pixels generate electrical charge, measured with 84-parts-per-million precision. Streams of digital brightness measurements flow continuously out as raw science data.

slides.slideTitle: Maintaining Precision and Discovering Distant Worlds
slides.text: Reaction wheels, hydrazine thrusters, and balanced sunlight pressure keep Kepler steady across all three axes. Raw pixel measurements pass through calibration and noise removal to build a clean light curve. Along that curve, a tiny recurring dip reveals a genuine transit signal. Automated vetting strips out false positives so real planetary candidates stand clear.

slides.title: MISSION CHALLENGES AND THE K2 REVIVAL
slides.sectionIntro: This part of Kepler's story reveals how even the most advanced spacecraft can face unexpected failures, and how engineering innovation can give a space mission a second life.
slides.slideTitle: Mission Challenges: When Kepler Lost Its Precision
slides.text: Kepler launched with four reaction wheels spinning in balance to hold the spacecraft steady. In July 2012, the first reaction wheel failed, leaving three to carry the load. In May 2013, a second reaction wheel failed. With only two wheels remaining, Kepler began to wobble and drift off its pointing as the starfield jittered. The telescope had lost the fine pointing precision required for its primary mission.

slides.title: MISSION CHALLENGES AND THE K2 REVIVAL
slides.slideTitle: The K2 Revival: Engineering a Second Mission
slides.text: Engineers aligned Kepler along the ecliptic plane so sunlight pressure balanced gently against the spacecraft. Working with the two remaining reaction wheels and brief thruster puffs, solar pressure restored stability. Reborn as K2, Kepler scanned successive fields along the ecliptic in 80-day observing campaigns. Across 19 campaigns, K2 continued discovering new worlds for four more years. After running out of propellant, Kepler retired on October 30, 2018.
